issues.legal_issue: A decree concerning immovable property requires registration when it creates a new present right rather than merely declaring a pre-existing right.
material_facts: The decree purported to make the claimant owner in possession of the property after the defendant’s death, although the claimant had no pre-existing right declared by the decree.
The property was the subject matter of the earlier suit, and the decree was not registered.
issues.conclusion: The exception for court decrees does not exempt a decree that creates a new present right in immovable property from compulsory registration; a decree that merely declares a pre-existing right is treated differently.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 17(1) and 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act, 1908, the exception for a court decree, including a compromise decree, covers a decree declaring a pre-existing right, but not one creating a new present right in immovable property. The court must examine whether the decree records an unqualified present disposition of rights. This accords with Tek Bahadur v. Debi Singh and Maturi Pullaiah v. Maturi Narasimham, which distinguish a document recording an arrangement from one creating rights, and Ratan Lal Sharma v. Purshottam Harit, which requires registration where a decree creates rights in immovable property.

predicates.proceeding_tests_registration_of_court_d: A party asks a court to determine whether a decree concerning property must be registered.
predicates.decree_creates_new_present_right: The decree itself gives a party a present right that the party did not already hold.
predicates.immovable_property_meets_registration_th: The decree concerns immovable property of a kind and value for which registration is compulsory.

issues.definition: When a proceeding tests registration of a court decree and the decree itself creates a new present right in qualifying immovable property, the decree requires registration.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered decree based on an admission cannot establish a claimed title when it creates that title for the first time.
material_facts: The earlier suit was disposed of because the defendant admitted the claimant’s asserted right, rather than through a compromise under which the suit was settled.
The decree purported to create the claimant’s right for the first time and was not registered.
The lower courts found the decree collusive and concluded that it was intended to defeat the bona fide claims of others to the property.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decree required registration and could not support the claimed title because it was unregistered. The decree was based on an admission under Order XII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, not a compromise under Order XXIII Rule 3; the petition was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A decree based on an admission under Order XII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure is distinct from a decree recording a compromise under Order XXIII Rule 3. In either event, a decree that creates a new present right in immovable property attracts the registration requirement in section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908. A bona fide decree declaring pre-existing rights may fall within section 17(2)(vi), but that exception does not protect a decree used to create a new right or evade registration requirements.

rule.if: proceeding_challenges_title_based_on_prior_decree and prior_suit_resolved_on_admission and decree_creates_right_for_first_time and decree_is_unregistered

predicates.proceeding_challenges_title_based_on_pri: A party to a later proceeding relies on an earlier court decree as the basis for a claimed title.
predicates.prior_suit_resolved_on_admission: The earlier suit was disposed of because a party admitted the opposing claim, rather than by recording a compromise.
predicates.decree_creates_right_for_first_time: The earlier decree purports to give a party a right that the party did not previously hold.
predicates.decree_is_unregistered: The earlier decree was not registered.

issues.definition: When a title challenge concerns an unregistered decree that resolved an earlier suit on an admission and created the claimed right for the first time, the decree does not confer that title.
